explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says to sing to the LORD, bless His name, and "proclaim His salvation day after day." Day after day, no days off. That's a lot of proclaiming, and I think it's a good kind of busy, like an oven that never gets cold.
Good guess, friend, since covenant is a big Bible word. But this verse doesn't say it. The writer says to "proclaim His salvation day after day." Salvation is the one to hold onto here.

Commands are a fair thing to think of, but they're not in this verse. After "bless His name," the writer says to "proclaim His salvation day after day." So the thing to proclaim is His salvation. Easy to mix up when the verse is moving fast.
That's it, friend. The writer says, "Declare His glory among the nations, His wonders among all peoples." Not just one little corner of the map. I'd say this is a very big announcement.

Close, because priests do show up in plenty of Bible places. But not here. The verse says, "Declare His glory among the nations, His wonders among all peoples." The nations are the ones hearing about it.

Elders are respectable folks, but this verse isn't aimed at them. It says, "Declare His glory among the nations, His wonders among all peoples." The word is nations, and the verse follows it right away with all peoples.

Right, friend. The writer says, "He is to be feared above all gods." It comes right after "great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised." So the LORD is greatly praised and above all gods, and the verse says both in one breath.

This one is true, friend. Psalm 96:4 says, "For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods." So the writer does say it, word for word. I know it sounds big, but the text is clear.
Yes, friend. The writer says, "all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens." Idols on one side, the One who made the heavens on the other. That's quite a contrast.
Not angels, friend. The writer doesn't call the gods of the nations angels at all. He says, "all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens."
Kings are a fun guess, but the verse says something else. It says, "all the gods of the nations are idols." Then it points to the LORD, who made the heavens. Idols is the word the writer picks.
Careful, friend, this one is false. The writer says, "Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and beauty fill His sanctuary." Fill is the word. Nothing about empty, and nothing about plain.
Right, friend. The psalm says, "Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and beauty fill His sanctuary." Fill, not empty. Strength and beauty are in there, so plain doesn't fit at all.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength." He says ascribe twice, so he really means it. I think he wants the families of the nations to hear it loud and clear.
Those are good things, friend, but they aren't the ones here. The writer says, "ascribe to the LORD glory and strength." Glory and strength is the pair in this verse.

That sounds like it could fit, friend, and it's a nice pair. But this verse says, "ascribe to the LORD glory and strength." The writer calls out to the families of the nations, and glory and strength is what he tells them to ascribe.
Not quite, friend. The writer says, "bring an offering and enter His courts." Enter, not wait outside. The verse invites them in.
Right, friend. Psalm 96:8 says, "Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; bring an offering and enter His courts." The verse has them going in, with no waiting outside.
Yes, friend. The writer says, "Declare among the nations: 'The LORD reigns!'" It's short and it has an exclamation point. That's a headline you can say in three words.
That's a comforting thing to say, friend, but it isn't the line here. The writer says, "Declare among the nations: 'The LORD reigns!'" Reigns is the word.
A lovely thing to say, friend, but not what this verse says. The announcement is, "The LORD reigns!" That's what the writer wants declared among the nations.

That's it, friend. The writer says, "The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved." Firmly established and cannot be moved go together. I'd call that solid, like a cookie sheet that doesn't wobble.
Judging does show up in this verse, friend, but later and about the peoples. Here the writer says the world "is firmly established; it cannot be moved." The word you want is moved.
Measuring is a decent guess, but the verse doesn't say it. The writer says the world "is firmly established; it cannot be moved." Moved is what it can't be.

Other way around, friend. The writer says, "Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it." Glad, rejoice and resound are not silent words. Nobody's whispering in this verse.

Right, friend. Psalm 96:11 says, "Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it." Heavens glad, earth rejoicing and the sea resounding is a long way from silent.

explanations.answer: He is coming to judge the earth
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writer says the trees sing for joy "before the LORD, for He is coming—He is coming to judge the earth." The reason is right there in the verse. The trees sing because He is coming.

explanations.answer: The harvest has finally come in
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice reason for singing, friend, but the writer never says it. He says the trees sing for joy "before the LORD, for He is coming—He is coming to judge the earth." His coming is the reason.

explanations.answer: The long winter is finally over
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a forest, friend, but winter isn't in this psalm. The writer says the trees sing "before the LORD, for He is coming—He is coming to judge the earth." That's the reason the verse gives.
